newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Election violence unlikely to affect leadership.
newsitem.headline: Election violence unlikely to affect leadership.

text.p: The violence that rocked parts of Indonesia in the final days of its general election campaign is unlikely to have any immediate effect on the country's future leadership, political analysts said on Monday.

The world's fourth most populous nation saw some of the worst political street violence of Suharto's 30-year rule during the campaign. But analysts said the most deadly incident, in which more than 130 people died in a shopping mall fire in remote South Kalimantan, was an isolated one. Indonesia was calm on Monday mid-way through a five-day cooling off period before 125 million eligible voters go to the polls on Thursday.

"This election is not about a mandate for Suharto, it is an election choosing 425 parliamentary members. It is not about casting a vote to give a new mandate to Suharto," a senior Asian diplomat said.

Suharto is now the world's second-longest serving leader after Cuba's Fidel Castro, replacing Zaire's ousted Mobutu Sese Seko for the number two spot. But the diplomat played down comparisons to the downfall of Mobutu and any threat to Suharto's rule.

"That's a very superficial kind of argument. The situation is entirely different," he said. Diplomats and political analysts said the most important election comes in March next year in a presidential poll in which Suharto is widely expected to run for a seventh five-year term of office. The question of a running-mate and potential successor to the 75-year-old leader is a key issue for the political and economic future of the country of 200 million people.

So far Suharto has given no indication of who he favours for the vice-presidency. An increasing number of people, however, are looking at the possibility of current Vice-President Try Sutrisno being accepted for an unprecedented second term.
Political analysts say there is a sense of uncertainty in the air as the country moves towards the new millennium and an eventual change in leadership.
Some say this has helped fuel isolated riots over the past year, blamed in part on socio-economic disparities and tensions, and pervasive corruption.
The election violence, analysts said, could be seen as the result of a combination of political partisanship, dissatisfaction and dissent with the government and youthful exuberance.

Dewi Fortuna Anwar, an analyst with the Centre for Information and Technology Studies (CIDES), noted that most demonstrators were youngsters seeing political activity for the first time -- political activism is banned during the five years between elections.
"A lot of them have never really experienced political participation, and the election campaign seems to be the only time they can let go," she told Reuters.

She said the emphasis on physical participation and the lack of substance in the campaign was a disappointment. "We really can't blame the people because they really haven't had much political experience. It is a reflection of our state of political maturity," she said.
Political commentator Mochtar Buchori said the whole concept of party politics was something new for many Indonesians, especially in rural areas.
"This whole game of general elections is something new for the public. They know how to elect personalities, but not parties," he said.

"In the past, they voted for the village head. Now they must make decisions about parties about which they know nothing," he said, adding that there was a general feeling that appointed officials were more important than elected officials.
He also said that the 17-to-24 age group was the most daring generation when it came to expressing concerns -- which included poverty and unemployment.
Analysts said one disturbing factor for the government was that hundreds of thousands of people had demonstrated in defiance of orders to keep campaigning off the streets.
"The key issue is whether the youngsters will get off the streets and go home after the elections," one Western diplomat commented.
Referring to the prospects for change after 30 years of rule by Suharto, who has raised the country from a poverty-stricken nation to one of Asia's "tiger" economies, he added:
"People don't want to fundamentally change the system, but they feel it is time for the system to move along."
